newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark, Russia, agree to differ on NATO growth.
newsitem.headline: Denmark, Russia, agree to differ on NATO growth.

text.p: Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen and his Russian counterpart Yevgeny Primakov ended talks on NATO expansion on Wednesday with the visitor adamant that Moscow would never drop its opposition.
Petersen believed a compromise could be reached.

Speaking at a joint news conference, Petersen, current chairman of the Organisation for Security and Co-Operation in Europe (OSCE), said that plans to offer former Soviet-bloc states membership in NATO posed no threat to Russia.
"The NATO which is developing is a new NATO...NATO wants a special relationship with Russia," he said.

"I believe that with good will on both sides an agreement can be reached which satisfies both parties," he said but added that there was no point trying to hide the two sides' present differences on the expansion issue.
Russia has repeatedly said that it cannot tolerate the alliance expanding on its borders and that a unilateral decision to do so by NATO would seriously damage future relations.
"We do not want any dividing lines in Europe and NATO enlargement would create such lines...we will never change our position on NATO enlargement," Primakov said.
Denmark is a leading advocate of NATO membership for the former Soviet Baltic republics of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Although Danish officials admit privately that there is little chance of the Balts joining in the first wave, expected to be announced at a July NATO summit in Madrid, they want to ensure that the door will not be closed in future.
"The first must not be the last," Helveg has said.

Primakov was dismissive of the Baltic states' prospects of ever joining the alliance, which is expected to invite Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic to be the first former Warsaw Pact members to join their erstwhile adversary.
"I think it will not happen," he said.

On Wednesday Danish analysts said that the Baltic nations themselves had to work to improve their strained relations with Moscow, citing guarantees of political rights for Russian minorities as one necessary step.

"The Baltic countries cannot imagine that they can sit there with policies which are provocative toward Russia. The Balts should be aware that their future lies not only in co-operation with the West but equally with Russia," Bertel Heurlin, of the Danish Institute of International Affairs, wrote in the Berlingske Tidende daily.

"It should be absolutely clear to the Balts that they need to fulfill several conditions before they can join NATO or the EU," added Joergen Estrup, foreign affairs spokesman for the Radical Liberals in Denmark's coalition government.
"Among other things they need to work for proper relations with Russia. Unfortunately the Balts do not always understand this requirement," he said.

Primakov's Danish visit is part of a tour which has already taken in Belgium, where he met NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, and Norway, the only alliance member to share a land border with Russia.

Alliance sources said that the Brussels meeting made progress on overall Russia-NATO relations although enlargement remained a thorny issue. On Thursday Primakov continues to London for talks with British leaders.
